lead: Measurement is not a passive look at a qubit. It is an interaction that forces one outcome from a set, with probabilities fixed by the state. For projective measurement the Born rule gives p(m)=⟨ψ|P_m|ψ⟩, and the state becomes P_m|ψ⟩/√p_m. This rule is the bridge from amplitudes to observed bits. It is used whenever a quantum algorithm reads a result, when a detector clicks in a lab, and when an error-correction circuit measures a stabiliser.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.1 and Chapter 2.3; Unit 1 inner products.

blocks.text: A measurement basis is a complete set of orthonormal states {|m⟩}. For each outcome m, the projector is P_m=|m⟩⟨m|. A projector is Hermitian and idempotent: P_m<sup>†</sup>=P_m and P_m<sup>2</sup>=P_m. Different outcomes have orthogonal projectors, P_mP_n=0 for m≠n, and they sum to identity, Σ_m P_m=I.

For a unit state |ψ⟩, the probability of outcome m is p(m)=⟨ψ|P_m|ψ⟩=|⟨m|ψ⟩|<sup>2</sup>. This is the Born rule. The number ⟨m|ψ⟩ is the amplitude for m; square its modulus to get probability. Probabilities are real, lie between 0 and 1, and sum to 1.

blocks.where: p(m) is the probability of outcome m; |ψ⟩ is the unit state; P_m=|m⟩⟨m| is the projector onto basis state |m⟩; ⟨m|ψ⟩ is the amplitude.

blocks.text: If the outcome is m, the state after measurement is |ψ_m⟩=P_m|ψ⟩/√p_m. For a basis projector this equals |m⟩ up to a phase. The division by √p_m renormalises the state to unit length. If p_m=0, outcome m cannot occur and the update is undefined.

You may measure in any orthonormal basis. In the computational basis {|0⟩,|1⟩}, projectors are P_0=|0⟩⟨0| and P_1=|1⟩⟨1|. In the X basis {|+⟩,|−⟩}, with |+⟩=(|0⟩+|1⟩)/√2 and |−⟩=(|0⟩−|1⟩)/√2, projectors are P_+=|+⟩⟨+| and P_−=|−⟩⟨−|.

To find probabilities, compute inner products with the new basis. For |ψ⟩=a|0⟩+b|1⟩, p(+)=|(a+b)/√2|<sup>2</sup> and p(−)=|(a−b)/√2|<sup>2</sup>. The state after outcome + is |+⟩; after − is |−⟩. A measurement in the X basis is also called an X measurement; on the Bloch sphere it asks for the spin along the x-axis.

Basis choice matters. Measuring |0⟩ in the Z basis gives 0 with probability 1. Measuring the same |0⟩ in the X basis gives + or − with probability 1/2 each. The state is not changed by a vague look; it is projected onto the chosen basis.

Projective measurement is the standard postulate, but a more general measurement is a positive operator-valued measure (POVM). It is a set of positive operators {E_m} with Σ_m E_m=I. The probability of outcome m is p(m)=⟨ψ|E_m|ψ⟩. Projective measurement is the special case E_m=P_m with P_m<sup>2</sup>=P_m and P_mP_n=0. General POVM elements may be non-orthogonal and need not be projectors.

POVMs describe noisy detectors and measurements where the system is not fully known. They do not give a simple collapse to E_m|ψ⟩ in the same way. A POVM is a bookkeeping device for probabilities; it may not specify the post-measurement state. POVM details are rarely examined in this unit; most exam questions use projective measurements. Open systems and measurement disturbance are left to advanced courses and to Chapter 2.9.

blocks.where: E_m is a positive operator for outcome m; I is the identity operator; p(m) is the outcome probability.

examples.question: A qubit is in state |ψ⟩ = (√3/2)|0⟩ + (1/2)|1⟩. It is measured in the {|+⟩,|−⟩} basis, with |+⟩=(|0⟩+|1⟩)/√2 and |−⟩=(|0⟩−|1⟩)/√2. (a) Find p(+) and p(−). (b) Give the state after each outcome.
steps: Write the amplitudes: a=√3/2 for |0⟩ and b=1/2 for |1⟩.
Check the probabilities sum to one: (2+√3)/4 + (2−√3)/4 = 4/4 = 1.
After outcome +: P_+|ψ⟩/√p(+) = |+⟩ because the amplitude is positive. After outcome −: P_−|ψ⟩/√p(−) = |−⟩.
examples.answer: p(+)=(2+√3)/4≈0.933 and p(−)=(2−√3)/4≈0.067. The states after the outcomes are |+⟩ and |−⟩ respectively.
examples.check:
import math
p_plus = (2 + math.sqrt(3)) / 4
p_minus = (2 - math.sqrt(3)) / 4
print(f"{p_plus:.3f}")
print(f"{p_minus:.3f}")

traps: Forgetting to divide by √p_m, leaving a subnormalised state.
Assuming measurement leaves |ψ⟩ unchanged; projective measurement changes it unless |ψ⟩ is already an eigenstate.
Mixing bases: computing p(+) with Z-basis projectors or using p(+) for the Z outcome.
Writing a probability greater than 1 after squaring the wrong amplitude or dropping the modulus.

quiz.q: State the Born rule for a projective measurement with projectors P_m.
quiz.a: p(m)=⟨ψ|P_m|ψ⟩=|⟨m|ψ⟩|²; the state after outcome m is P_m|ψ⟩/√p_m.

quiz.q: Why is the collapsed state divided by √p_m?
quiz.a: To make its norm 1. P_m|ψ⟩ has norm √p_m, so division restores a valid unit state.

quiz.q: A qubit is |0⟩. It is measured in the X basis. Find p(+), p(−), and the state after each outcome.
Measure |ψ⟩=(1/√2)|0⟩+(1/√2)|1⟩ in the Z basis. Find probabilities and post-measurement states.
P_m and P_n are orthogonal projectors. Outcome m has just occurred. What is the probability of outcome n in an immediate repeat measurement, and why?
quiz.a: 0, because P_nP_m=0, so P_n applied to collapsed state |m⟩ gives zero.

quiz.q: Give one difference between a projective measurement and a general POVM.
quiz.a: Projective uses orthogonal projectors P_m with P_m²=P_m; POVM uses positive E_m with ΣE_m=I that may be non-orthogonal and non-projective.

quiz.q: For a state |ψ⟩, an outcome m has p_m=0. Can the state after measurement be P_m|ψ⟩/√p_m? Explain.
quiz.a: No. p_m=0 means the outcome cannot occur, so the conditional state is undefined. The formula divides by zero and is not physical.

quiz.q: What is P_m² for a projector?

beyond: Not for the exam. Measurement is the readout step in every quantum processor; hardware teams calibrate readout errors using POVMs and tomography. Quantum error correction repeatedly measures stabilisers, so the Born rule and collapse are part of the control software. Search next for quantum state tomography, readout fidelity, and stabiliser measurement.
